blocks.content: Endocrine System – Introduction

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Endocrine glands are ductless glands that release chemical messengers called hormones directly into the bloodstream.
The Hypothalamus acts as the control center, connecting the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland.
The Pancreas is a heterocrine gland functioning both as an exocrine gland (digestive enzymes) and an endocrine gland (insulin and glucagon).
Thyroxine secretion requires adequate iodine; deficiency causes Goitre and Hypothyroidism.
Adrenal glands produce cortisol and adrenaline to regulate stress responses, metabolism, and blood pressure.

blocks.content:
The endocrine system is a system of ductless glands that secrete chemical substances called hormones directly into the bloodstream.

These hormones regulate various physiological activities of the body.

Unlike the nervous system, the endocrine system acts slowly but its effects are long-lasting.

The endocrine system plays a vital role in growth, metabolism, reproduction, and maintenance of internal balance.

It works in close coordination with the nervous system to control and regulate body functions.
2. Hormones – Definition and Nature

Hormones are chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands.

They are released directly into the blood and carried to specific target organs.

Hormones are required in very small quantities but have powerful effects.

They regulate growth, development, metabolism, and reproduction.

Hormones can be protein, steroid, or amine in nature.

Each hormone has a specific target and function.
3. Difference Between Endocrine and Exocrine Glands

Endocrine glands are ductless glands that release hormones directly into the bloodstream.

Examples include pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, and pancreas.

Exocrine glands possess ducts and release secretions to body surfaces or cavities.

Examples include sweat glands, salivary glands, and digestive glands.
4. Hypothalamus

The hypothalamus is a small but important part of the brain.

It acts as a link between the nervous system and the endocrine system.

It controls the secretion of hormones from the pituitary gland.

Hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, and sleep.

It plays a key role in maintaining homeostasis.
Endocrine glands are ductless glands that secrete chemical messengers known as hormones directly into the blood stream to regulate target organ functions.
5. Pituitary Gland

The pituitary gland is known as the master gland of the endocrine system.

It is located at the base of the brain.

It controls the activity of other endocrine glands.

The pituitary gland has two lobes: anterior and posterior.

Hormones secreted by the pituitary regulate growth, reproduction, and metabolism.
6. Growth Hormone

Growth hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland.

It regulates growth and development of bones and muscles.

Excess secretion of growth hormone in childhood leads to gigantism.

Deficiency of growth hormone causes dwarfism.

In adults, excess growth hormone leads to acromegaly.
7. Thyroid Gland

The thyroid gland is located in the neck region, in front of the trachea.

It secretes thyroxine hormone.

Thyroxine regulates metabolism, growth, and development.

Iodine is required for the synthesis of thyroxine.

Deficiency of iodine causes enlargement of thyroid gland known as goitre.

blocks.content: 8. Disorders of Thyroid Gland

Hypothyroidism occurs due to decreased secretion of thyroxine.

It leads to low metabolic rate, weight gain, and fatigue.

In children, hypothyroidism causes cretinism.

Hyperthyroidism occurs due to excess thyroxine.

It leads to increased metabolism, weight loss, and nervousness.
9. Pancreas

Pancreas is a mixed gland with both endocrine and exocrine functions.

As an endocrine gland, it secretes insulin and glucagon.

Insulin regulates blood sugar level by lowering it.

Glucagon increases blood sugar level.

Deficiency of insulin leads to diabetes mellitus.
10. Adrenal Glands

Adrenal glands are located above the kidneys.

They secrete hormones such as adrenaline, aldosterone, and cortisol.

Adrenaline prepares the body for emergency situations.

It increases heart rate, blood pressure, and blood glucose level.

Adrenal glands help the body cope with stress.
11. Parathyroid Glands

items: Pituitary gland is known as the 'Master Gland' of the human body, but its own function is controlled by the Hypothalamus.
Adrenaline is widely referred to as the 'Fight, Flight, or Fright' (3F) emergency hormone.
Insulin deficiency leads to Diabetes Mellitus, whereas deficiency of ADH (Vasopressin) leads to Diabetes Insipidus.
Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas contain Beta cells that secrete Insulin and Alpha cells that secrete Glucagon.

blocks.content:
Parathyroid glands are located behind the thyroid gland.

They secrete parathormone.

Parathormone regulates calcium and phosphorus levels in the blood.

Deficiency of parathormone causes muscle cramps and tetany.

Excess secretion leads to weak bones.
12. Gonads

Gonads are sex glands.

In males, testes secrete testosterone.

In females, ovaries secrete estrogen and progesterone.

These hormones control development of secondary sexual characters.

They also regulate reproductive functions.
13. IMPORTANT FACTS –  FOCUS

• Endocrine glands are ductless.

• Hormones are chemical messengers.

• Pituitary is the master gland.

• Growth hormone controls body growth.

• Thyroxine regulates metabolism.

• Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone.

• Insulin deficiency causes diabetes.

• Adrenaline is emergency hormone.

• Parathormone regulates calcium.

• Testosterone is male sex hormone.
